query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporate a Ti precursor along with a carbon source into the starting powder mixture to promote the in‐situ formation of uniformly distributed TiC precipitates at the W–Cu interface, thereby sealing the gap and enhancing thermal conduction.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix that suffers from phase separation and interfacial voids during high heat flux and irradiation exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low concentration of Ti (e.g., 2–3 wt%) along with an appropriate carbon source (adjusted to yield an approximate 1:1 molar ratio with Ti) into the starting powders prior to spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Sinter under high-temperature SPS conditions (e.g., 800 °C for 10 minutes) in an inert atmosphere, followed by service under conditions relevant to plasma-facing and Cu-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: In‐situ formed, uniformly dispersed TiC precipitates decorating the W/Cu interfaces.
generation.mechanism: During sintering, Ti reacts with the carbon source to form TiC particles that nucleate and grow at the W–Cu interface. These precipitates fill voids and act as a bonding layer, reducing interfacial energy mismatches and establishing continuous thermal pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: A composite with significantly reduced interfacial voids and phase separation, resulting in a higher thermal conductivity and improved mechanical integrity under irradiation.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite displaying notable phase separation and interfacial voids when subjected to combined heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is effective if the TiC phase forms uniformly and remains stable under service temperatures (typically below 1500 °C) and irradiation doses. Excessive carbide formation must be avoided by strict control of the Ti/carbon ratio.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed molar ratio aims for optimal TiC formation, the exact volume fraction required for maximum thermal conductivity improvement needs further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one with the Ti and carbon addition (using the specified Ti:carbon ratio) and one without. Maintain identical SPS conditions for both sets.
measurements: Utilize high-resolution TEM/EDS to assess the formation, distribution, and uniformity of TiC at the W–Cu interface.
Perform thermal conductivity measurements under simulated high-flux heat and irradiation conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added composites do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in interfacial voids or an improvement in thermal conductivity and interfacial stability when compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: The W-based composite having uniformly distributed TiC within the grains and along the grain boundaries can withstand heat flux as high as 200 MW/m2, which is nearly 100% higher than the flux sustained by pure W. An increase in the amount of the evenly distributed TiC in the W matrix (inside the grains and along the boundaries) also increases the hardness creep strength and modulus of elasticity, , . The presence of TiC in the grains and on the grain boundaries also favors fusion applications, as it increases the recrystallization temperature and irradiation resistance. TiC does not have a significant effect on the deuterium retention behavior of W-based materials, . The dispersion of carbides in the grain boundaries of W leads to grain boundary strengthening and provides some resistance to grain boundary migration at elevated temperatures. Therefore, TiC is considered to be beneficial in high-temperature and plasma-facing alloys. candidates.hypothesis: Incorporate a minor fraction of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) additive into the Cu matrix to form a chemically graded interphase with the W phase.

candidates.hypothesis: Utilize a rapid liquid phase-assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering process to transiently form an interfacial liquid that enables defect-free densification at the W–Cu boundary.
candidates.intervention: Adopt an ultrahigh-temperature sintering method that rapidly heats the composite (approaching transient liquid-stage temperatures, e.g., near 3000 K for a short duration) to induce a fleeting liquid phase at the interface, followed by rapid cooling.

candidates.hypothesis: Pre-coat tungsten particles with a thin Ti/Ni interlayer to enhance the wettability and interfacial bonding with the Cu matrix, thereby preventing phase separation and void formation.
candidates.intervention: Apply a thin, conformal Ti/Ni coating on tungsten particles using magnetron sputtering prior to composite fabrication followed by spark plasma sintering.
